items.title: A title and its tasks
items.prose: An invented London firm posts an internship titled "Quantitative Trader". Read what the intern will do.

columns: The posting says the intern will
rows: Maintain the C++ gateway that sends orders to the exchange
Fix faults in the live trading system

state.caption: An invented firm. The tasks are what matter.

items.question: You have three weeks before the first round. What should you prepare?

options.text: Coding at speed and data structures, with C++ and systems
Mental arithmetic, probability and market-making games
options.why: You prepared for the title. Every task listed is building or fixing code, which is a developer's day.

options.text: Statistics, regression and an open data case
options.why: You prepared a researcher's rounds. None of the tasks is testing ideas on data.

options.text: Derivatives pricing and this month's market news
options.why: You prepared finance knowledge. Trading firms state none is needed, and these tasks need code.

feedback.correct: The tasks are a developer's, so expect coding rounds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the tasks, not the title, then take that role's tests.

explain.text: Maintaining an order gateway, cutting its response time and fixing live faults are a developer's tasks. The tasks tell you the role, and the role tells you the tests. A title alone can point the wrong way.

items.title: Matching the firm to the day
items.prose: You want to quote prices all day with the firm's own money at risk. You also want to know the same day whether you were right.
items.question: Which internship fits that best?

options.text: A trading role at a proprietary trading firm or market maker
A research role at a hedge fund
options.why: You picked a fund. A hedge fund invests outside investors' money and holds positions for days or weeks.

options.text: A strats role at a bank
options.why: You picked a bank desk. Strats build models and tools for desks that mostly serve clients.

options.text: Any of them, since the kind of firm makes no difference
options.why: You ignored the firm type. Whose money is traded, and how often, changes the daily work.

feedback.correct: A trading firm trades its own money, and its traders quote all day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whose money is at risk, and how fast the feedback comes.

explain.text: A proprietary trading firm risks only its own money, and its traders quote prices all day. A hedge fund invests for outside investors and holds positions longer. Bank strats build models and code for desks that mostly serve clients.

items.title: Counting to a deadline
items.prose: Today is 2 November 2026. An invented firm's spring week closes on 10 January 2027 and reviews applications on a rolling basis.
items.question: How many days are left until it closes?

feedback.correct: 28 days of November, 31 of December, then 10: 69.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the rest of November, then all of December, then the days into January.

byKey.incl: You counted today as well. 10 January is 69 days after 2 November.
byKey.no-dec: You skipped December. Its 31 days sit between the end of November and 10 January.
byKey.no-nov: You started from 1 December. November still has 28 days left after the 2nd.

explain.text: November has 28 days left after the 2nd, December has 31, and January adds 10: $28 + 31 + 10 = 69$. As a check, 2 November plus 59 days is 31 December, and 10 more is 10 January. Under rolling review the closing date is the last day, not the target.

items.title: Lines with nothing behind them
items.prose: A student's draft CV, one line per row. Any line can become an interview question. Scroll the table to the end.

rows: Driven, detail-oriented self-starter with a passion for markets
Simulated a dice market in Python; checked 8 expected values against exact answers
Duties included helping the analytics team
Cut a weekly stock count from 5 hours to 2 with a spreadsheet macro
Familiar with a wide range of programming languages
Bridge: county under-21 team for 3 seasons

items.question: Tap the four lines to cut or rewrite before the CV goes out.

feedback.correct: The profile, the duty, the vague skills line and the generic interests.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the lines with no fact, number or result an interviewer could ask about.

byKey.r1: A predicted grade and an average are facts the university can confirm.
byKey.r2: Eight expected values checked against exact answers is a claim an interviewer can probe.
byKey.r4: That line has a before, an after and a tool. Expect "how?", and it has an answer.
byKey.r6: A team and three seasons can be checked. Expect a question about bridge.

explain.text: The four lines give an adjective, a duty, a vague claim and interests true of almost everyone. Every other line holds a fact, a number or a result to ask about. Rewrite the duty as something you did, with a tool and a number.

items.title: The first sentence on camera
items.prose: A recorded question appears: "Tell us about a time you made a mistake." You have about 30 seconds to prepare, then about 2 minutes on camera.
items.question: Which first sentence is best?

options.text: "In my second-year group project, I sent the team the wrong dataset two days before the deadline."
"Everyone makes mistakes; what matters is how you learn from them."
options.why: You opened with a general view. The reviewer asked for a time, and the clock is already running.

options.text: "Thank you for this opportunity; I'm really excited to be here."
options.why: You opened with thanks. It spends seconds of a single take and answers nothing.

options.text: "My biggest mistake is that I'm a perfectionist."
options.why: You picked a strength in disguise. Reviewers hear it as a dodge, and it names no time.

feedback.correct: It names one real time, so the answer has started.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the sentence that starts the story at once.

explain.text: The best first sentence names one real time, so the reviewer knows the answer has begun. Then one story for about 80 seconds, and a close on the role for 30. A warm-up or a disguised strength wastes the one take.

items.title: Saying the plan
items.prose: Interviewer: "Two fair dice. What is the chance the total is at least 10?"
items.question: Which reply lets the interviewer follow and check you?

options.text: "So a total of 10, 11 or 12. I'll count cells: 3, 2 and 1 of 36. That's 6 of 36, so 1/6."
Think in silence for a minute, then say "1/6"
options.why: You went silent. The answer is right, but the interviewer saw no method to mark or steer.

options.text: "Ten... three... two, one... six... thirty-six... a sixth."
options.why: You narrated digits with no plan. The listener cannot tell which number is which.

options.text: "I haven't seen this one before, sorry."
options.why: You stopped. Say what you know and the plan you would try; this one is a count.

feedback.correct: Restate, plan, count, answer: every step can be checked.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the reply that says the plan before the numbers.

explain.text: The strong reply restates the question and names the plan, a count of cells. Totals of 10, 11 and 12 take 3, 2 and 1 of the 36 cells, so $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$. Each line can be checked, and the interviewer could step in at any one.

items.title: Which cycle is hers?
items.prose: Today is 2 November 2026. Priya is in the third year of a four-year MMath, graduating in 2028. She has not applied anywhere yet.
items.question: What should she do this week?

options.text: Apply at once to the summer 2027 internships still open
Apply for a spring week this cycle
options.why: You gave her the wrong programme. Spring weeks are for students two years from graduation; she is one year away.

options.text: Wait for the postings that open in July 2027
options.why: You waited a cycle. Summer 2028 comes after she graduates, so summer 2027 is her main internship.

options.text: Wait until January, when this cycle's offers are settled
options.why: You waited for the offers. Under rolling review places fill as applications arrive, and most offers land by mid-December.

feedback.correct: Summer 2027 is her penultimate-year internship, and its places are filling now.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find her penultimate year, then where that cycle stands today.

explain.text: A four-year degree makes the third year the penultimate one, so summer 2027 is her main internship. Its postings opened in July and August 2026, and offers land until mid-December. Under rolling review she applies today to every role still open.

items.title: Pay quoted by the month
items.prose: An invented trading firm's offer quotes £12,000 a month for a 10-week summer internship. You want to compare it with a weekly figure from another offer.
items.question: What does it pay over the 10 weeks, to the nearest pound?

feedback.correct: Ten weeks is about 2.31 months: £27,692.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn the monthly figure into a year, then take 10 fifty-seconds of it.

byKey.four-week: You took a month as four weeks. A month is 52/12, about 4.33 weeks, so 10 weeks is under 2.5 months.
byKey.months: You treated 10 weeks as 10 months. Ten weeks is about 2.31 months.
byKey.one: That is one month. The internship runs for 10 weeks.

explain.text: A year has 12 months and 52 weeks, so 10 weeks is $\tfrac{120}{52} \approx 2.31$ months. $12{,}000 \times \tfrac{120}{52} \approx 27{,}692$ pounds. As a check, £144,000 a year is about £2,769 a week, and 10 of those make £27,692.

items.title: A research process into a list
items.prose: Firm R is an invented hedge fund. Its careers page describes its research internship process.

rows: After you apply, you sit a 90-minute coding test on a dataset.
Pass it, and a researcher calls you for 45 minutes of statistics and probability.
The final day has three technical interviews and one behavioural interview.

items.question: Select all that apply: what goes on your preparation list?

options.text: Python coding on data, such as a regression
Statistics and probability questions
Behavioural stories in STAR form
An 80-item arithmetic battery under negative marking
options.why: You carried over a trading firm's speed test. Firm R's first test is coding on data.

options.text: A live market-making game
options.why: You prepared for a trader's process. Nothing on Firm R's page is a trading game.

options.text: C++ memory management
options.why: You prepared for a developer's systems round. Firm R's coding test is on a dataset.

feedback.correct: Coding on data, statistics and probability, and stories for the behavioural round.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only what each stage of the page tests.

explain.text: Each stage names what it tests, so the list writes itself: coding on data, statistics and probability, then stories. Speed batteries and games belong to trading processes. Pages change every cycle, so date the list and check it again before you apply.

items.title: Notes from last autumn
items.prose: In October 2026 you noted four facts about an invented trading firm. You apply next July.

rows: No retake of its test within 8 months
Two phone rounds, then a final day

items.question: Which plan is sound?

options.text: Confirm every fact on the firm's page, aim as high as you can, and prepare for a coding test
Plan to score exactly 55 net, the pass mark
options.why: You treated a prep-site guess as a pass mark. The sites disagree, so 55 may fall short.

options.text: Skip coding practice, since some reports say there is no test
options.why: You bet on the kinder report. Preparing for a test that never comes costs hours; missing one costs the application.

options.text: Trust the official line without checking, and drop the reported ones
options.why: You treated a dated note as current. Formats change every cycle, so every line is checked on the firm's page.

feedback.correct: A dated map, checked again, with the disputed stage prepared for.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how old each fact will be, and what each mistake would cost.

explain.text: Notes from October 2026 are a dated map, checked on the firm's own page before you apply. A pass mark from sites that disagree is not a target. A disputed stage is cheaper to prepare for than to miss.

items.title: Rewriting a duty
items.prose: At a summer job in an insurer's back office, you wrote a SQL query for the daily claims report. It cut the job from 2 hours to 15 minutes. Your draft line says "Helped with reporting".
items.question: Which line should replace it?

options.text: Automated the daily claims report in SQL, cutting it from 2 hours to 15 minutes
Helped with extensive, high-quality reporting across the business
options.why: You added adjectives. They give an interviewer nothing more to check.

options.text: Transformed the firm's reporting, saving it thousands of pounds
options.why: You claimed a result you cannot defend. One question about the thousands would expose it.

options.text: SQL, Excel, reporting, data
options.why: You wrote a list. It has tools but no verb, no task and no number.

feedback.correct: A verb, the task, the tool and a number you can defend.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the line you could explain step by step.

explain.text: The line has a verb, the task, the tool and a number you can defend. Two hours to 15 minutes is 8 times faster, and asked "how?" you can describe the query. Inflated or vague lines fail the first follow-up.

items.title: A London CV
items.prose: A friend's draft CV for London internships, top to bottom: a photo, her date of birth and a career objective. Then her café job, her two coding projects, and education with a predicted First. It runs to two pages.
items.question: Select all that apply: which changes does it need?

options.text: Cut it to one page
Remove the photo and the date of birth
Drop the career objective
Put education first, then the projects, then the café job
Remove the predicted First until it is achieved
options.why: You took the grade off. UK employers expect a predicted or achieved grade, and a gap looks like hiding it.

options.text: Drop the café job, since it is not finance
options.why: You hid real evidence. Keep the job below the projects, written for the skill it shows.

feedback.correct: One page, no photo or date of birth, no objective, education then projects.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the grade and the job; remove what says nothing about skill.

explain.text: A UK student CV is one page, with no photo and no date of birth. Education leads, then projects, then jobs written for the skill they show. A career objective is adjectives, and the predicted grade stays.

items.title: Why us, for a research role
items.prose: You apply for a quant research internship at an invented hedge fund. Here are four drafts of "Why us?".
items.question: Which answer is strongest?

options.text: "At your October campus talk, a researcher showed how you test signals on held-out years. My momentum note did that. I want weeks on one question like it."
"Your talk showed how you test signals on held-out years, and I wrote a momentum note. I like fast decisions, judged the same day."
options.why: You gave a trader's reason. Same-day feedback argues for a trading role, not research.

options.text: "You are the most selective fund on my list, and the pay is reported to be the best."
options.why: You led with prestige and pay. Interviewers hear "would leave for more", and it fits any firm.

options.text: "You are a world-leading, innovative fund that values integrity and teamwork."
options.why: You copied a careers page. Swap in another fund's name and it still works, so it says nothing.

feedback.correct: A true fact with its source, your evidence, and a research reason.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a fact, your own evidence and why this role.

explain.text: The strong answer has a true fact with its source, your own evidence and why this role. The second answer breaks the third part with a trader's reason. Swap in another firm's name: if an answer still works, it is generic.

items.title: One real attempt
items.prose: A proctored online test link arrives. The firm allows no retake within 8 months. Calculators are not allowed.
items.question: Select all that apply: which steps protect your one real attempt?

options.text: Practise on mocks, and on any practice test the firm offers
Run the platform's system check in the room you will use
Read the scoring and what is allowed on the desk before item 1
Close other tabs, charge the laptop and put the phone away
Open the real link once to see the format
options.why: You used the real link as practice. That sitting is your attempt, and its score stands for 8 months.

options.text: Sit it in a café, where the Wi-Fi is fast
options.why: You trusted public Wi-Fi. A dropped connection mid-test can end the attempt.

options.text: Do a full mock straight before the real one
options.why: You tired yourself first. Arrive fresh and do the last mock on an earlier day.

feedback.correct: Practice elsewhere, then the machine, the rules and the room.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the steps that protect the machine, the connection, the rules or the room.

explain.text: Every right step protects the machine, the connection, the rules or the room. The real link is never practice, because the first sitting counts. A proctored test may also flag a phone, a second screen or another person.

items.title: A slip on camera
items.prose: Seventy seconds into a two-minute recorded answer, you hear yourself say the project scored 87%. It was 78%. The platform allows one take.
items.question: What do you do?

options.text: Correct it in one clause, "sorry, 78%", and carry on with the story
Stop and look for a retake button
options.why: You hoped for a retake. Most platforms reportedly allow one take, and the clock keeps running.

options.text: Start the story again from the top
options.why: You restarted. Only 50 seconds are left, so the result and the close would be cut off.

options.text: Leave it, since the reviewer will not notice
options.why: You left a wrong number on the record. A live round may ask about it, and a fixed slip is marked well.

feedback.correct: Name it, fix it in one clause, carry on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You have one take and 50 seconds left.

explain.text: Fixing a slip in one clause is the recovery interviewers mark, recorded or live. With 50 of the 120 seconds left, restarting would lose the result and the close. Left alone, the wrong 87% stays on the record.

items.title: Three faults in one story
items.prose: An answer to "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision", one sentence a row.

rows: Last spring our society's committee planned to move the quiz night to a Friday.
I was events officer, and I thought Fridays were our weakest night.
We looked at the numbers and talked it through.
In the end it went really well.
I learned that I care too much about getting things right.

items.question: Select all that apply: which faults does the answer have?

options.text: Sentence 3 hides the candidate's actions inside "we"
Sentence 4 gives a result with no number or visible outcome
Sentence 5 is a strength in disguise, not a reflection
It describes a real past event instead of saying "I would"
options.why: You marked a strength as a fault. A real time, with when and who, is what the question asks for.

options.text: A society story cannot answer a quant interview question
options.why: You ruled out the setting. Interviewers mark the actions and the result, not where they happened.

feedback.correct: "We" for the actions, no number in the result, and a disguised strength.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the action, the result and the reflection.

explain.text: The actions need "I": "I pulled two years of attendance and showed the committee." The result needs a number, such as attendance against last year. A reflection names a real lesson, not a flattering flaw.

items.title: Catching your own slip
items.prose: You said aloud: "At least one six in two rolls: 1/6 plus 1/6, so 1/3." Two lines later you see that (6, 6) was counted twice.
items.question: What do you say?

options.text: "I counted (6, 6) twice. It's 1 minus 25/36, so 11/36. Carrying on."
"I counted (6, 6) twice, so it's 10/36."
options.why: You took the double count off twice. 12/36 holds (6, 6) twice, so remove it once: 11/36.

options.text: Say nothing and hope it is not noticed
options.why: You hid the slip. Interviewers usually see it, and then they mark the hiding.

options.text: Apologise at length, then start the question again in silence
options.why: You restarted in silence. Fix the one step aloud and keep the rest.

feedback.correct: Name the slip, give the right value, carry on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix the one step aloud, with the right number.

explain.text: Adding the two chances counts (6, 6) twice: $\tfrac{12}{36}$ less one cell is $\tfrac{11}{36}$. The complement agrees: $1 - \tfrac{25}{36} = \tfrac{11}{36}$. Interviewers report marking the recovery, so name it in one sentence and go on.

items.title: Expect a bad round
items.prose: A final day has five rounds. Suppose each goes badly with chance 0.15, independently. The 0.15 is an illustration, not a reported rate.
items.question: What is the chance that at least one round goes badly? Give three decimal places.

widget.label: Chance of at least one bad round

feedback.correct: $1 - 0.85^5 \approx 0.556$: more likely than not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that every round goes well, then take it from 1.

byKey.added: You added 5 × 0.15. That counts days with two bad rounds twice.
byKey.none: That is the chance every round goes well. Take it from 1.
byKey.four: You used four rounds. This day has five.

explain.text: No bad round needs all five to go well: $0.85^5 \approx 0.444$. So the chance of at least one bad round is $1 - 0.444 = 0.556$, more likely than not. Plan the 60-second reset before the day, not after the bad round.

items.title: Week six of ten
items.prose: Week 6 of a 10-week internship. Your own project is half done. Another team asks you to help with theirs as well.
items.question: What gives you the best chance of a return offer?

options.text: Say you will finish your own project first, then help if time allows
Join both projects, to show energy
options.why: You spread yourself thin. One project, owned and finished, is what is judged.

options.text: Move to their project, since their team is bigger
options.why: You dropped the project you own. A half-finished project gives the review nothing to judge.

options.text: Say yes to both, then work late every night until the end
options.why: You traded steady work for hours. Day 50 is judged like day 1, and tired work shows.

feedback.correct: One project, owned, finished and written up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the return-offer decision judges.

explain.text: Return offers go to interns who finish one project, present it and write it up clearly. Decisions come in the last weeks, so weeks 7 to 10 carry the write-up. Saying so politely shows you own your work.

items.title: After an automated rejection
items.prose: A trading firm rejects you after its online test on 20 November 2026, by automated email. Its rule is no retake within 8 months.
items.question: Put your steps in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: That day: write down the item types that cost you time
Name the skill the test exposed: speed under negative marking
Train it with Mental Maths Under Pressure, three sessions a week
Apply to that firm again once its wait ends, on 20 July 2027
Sit the test again next week with a new email address
lines.why: You planned a second account. The rule is no retake within 8 months, and a new address breaks it.

feedback.correct: Notes, the skill, the course, then the retry when the wait ends.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The plan needs the skill, and the skill needs your notes.

byKey.reset: You kept the second account. It breaks the 8-month rule and can void every application to that firm.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step that belongs. Only the new email address goes.

explain.text: Notes come the same day, while memory is fresh, and they point to one skill. The course trains it, and the retry waits for the rule: 8 months from 20 November 2026 is 20 July 2027. Other firms judge you fresh in the meantime.

items.title: Routes after a final round
items.prose: Leo is in a one-year MSc that ends in September 2027. In February 2027 a hedge fund turns him down for a summer research internship after its final round.
items.question: Select all that apply: which are real routes from here?

options.text: An off-cycle research role starting after his course ends
A research role at a bank or another fund that is still open
One short request to his recruiter for one area to work on
The same application to the same fund next week
options.why: You resent at once. Most firms keep a wait, and nothing in the application has changed.

options.text: A spring week, to stay in the cycle
options.why: You ignored eligibility. Spring weeks are for students two years from graduation.

options.text: No applications at all until next July
options.why: You paused everything. Other firms judge him fresh, and some roles stay open until filled.

feedback.correct: Off-cycle after the course, other firms, and one feedback request.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the routes that judge him fresh or teach him something.

explain.text: Off-cycle roles run 3 to 6 months outside the summer, so they suit him once the course ends. Other firms judge him fresh, and a named recruiter can pass on one area. The same fund usually wants a wait and a changed application.

items.title: Eligibility, then fit
items.prose: Omar is in the second year of a three-year BSc, graduating in 2028. He aims at research and can work only in the UK. Today is 2 November 2026. Scroll the table to the end.

rows: Penultimate year; Amsterdam, Dutch work permission

items.question: Tap every programme that passes both eligibility and fit for Omar.

feedback.correct: Two rows: the London research summer and the bank's quant research summer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check his year, then the track, the region and the timing.

byKey.r0: He is a second-year, so a first-year programme is closed to him.
byKey.r1: He graduates in 2028, so a class-of-2029 spring week is not his.
byKey.r3: This one expects a Master's degree or above.
byKey.r4: He aims at research and can work only in the UK.
byKey.r6: Six months from January falls in his term. Off-cycle roles suit a year out or a Master's.

explain.text: Eligibility removes the first-year week, the class-of-2029 spring week, the Master's role and the closed posting. Fit removes the Amsterdam trader role and the off-cycle role, which falls in his term. The bank's closes on 30 November, so it goes first.

items.title: More applications or better ones?
items.prose: Plan A: send 20 applications this month, each with a 5% chance of an offer. Plan B: spend two weeks on practice and the CV, then send 10, each at 12%. Treat the applications as independent.
items.question: Which plan leaves the lower chance of no offer?

options.text: Plan B: about 0.28, against about 0.36 for plan A
Plan A, because more applications always mean less risk
options.why: You counted only the number sent. $0.95^{20} \approx 0.36$ is above $0.88^{10} \approx 0.28$.

options.text: Plan A, since 20 × 5% is 100% and an offer is certain
options.why: You added the chances. They multiply: all twenty fail with chance about 0.36.

options.text: Neither, since both expect about one offer
options.why: You compared averages only. Plan B expects 1.2 offers to plan A's 1.0, and leaves less chance of none.

feedback.correct: Plan B: fewer, stronger applications leave less chance of none.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $(1 - p)^n$ for each plan.

explain.text: $P(\text{no offer}) = (1-p)^n$ gives $0.95^{20} \approx 0.358$ and $0.88^{10} \approx 0.279$. Real applications share one CV and one set of skills, so both figures are optimistic. Raising $p$ by preparing lifts every application at once.

items.title: When to guess
items.prose: A test has four options an item: +1 for right, −0.5 for wrong, 0 for a blank. Skipping is allowed. You cannot solve 14 items. On 8 of them you can rule out two options; on the other 6, none.
items.question: Under the best policy, what do those 14 items add to your expected score?

widget.label: Expected marks from the 14 items
widget.accept: 2 marks: guess on the 8, leave the 6 blank

feedback.correct: Guess on the 8, leave the 6 blank: 2 marks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what a guess is worth with two options left, and with four.

byKey.all: You guessed on all 14. Each blind guess loses 0.125 on average, so the 6 cost 0.75.
byKey.nopen: You left out the penalty. Half of the 8 guesses are wrong and cost 0.5 each.
byKey.skip: You skipped everything. With two options left a guess gains 0.25 on average.

explain.text: With two options left a guess is worth $\tfrac12 - \tfrac12 \times 0.5 = 0.25$, so the 8 add $8 \times 0.25 = 2$. A blind guess is worth $\tfrac14 - \tfrac34 \times 0.5 = -0.125$, so the 6 stay blank. Guessing on all 14 would give $2 - 0.75 = 1.25$.

items.title: The rest of the day
items.prose: Your final day has four rounds with 15-minute gaps between them. Round 2 has just gone badly.
items.question: Select all that apply: which moves are sound?

options.text: In the gap: water, one slow breath, one written line on what to fix, then put it away
Answer round 3's "How's the day going?" with a short, true, positive line
Tell round 4's interviewer you have seen their puzzle, then solve it aloud
Ask an interviewer what interns own and how feedback is given
Open round 3 by explaining what went wrong in round 2
options.why: You carried round 2 in. The new interviewer had no view of it, and now expects a weak round.

options.text: Replay round 2 in your head during the gap, to learn from it
options.why: You spent the gap reliving it. The lesson can wait for the evening, when it costs nothing.

options.text: Ask round 4's interviewer about the starting bonus
options.why: You asked about pay. That is for the recruiter, once you hold an offer.

feedback.correct: Reset in the gap, start each round at zero, be honest, ask about the work.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each round is marked on its own; keep the moves that start the next one at zero.

explain.text: Each round is usually marked on its own, so round 3 starts at zero. The reset parks round 2 in one line, and honesty about a seen puzzle is marked. Questions about the work suit interviewers; pay waits for the recruiter.

items.title: Two offers, one condition
items.prose: You want a full-time trading job. You can work in the UK, but you have not checked the Netherlands. You are predicted a First.

rows: Right to work in the Netherlands

items.question: What should you do first?

options.text: Check the Netherlands work condition now, asking A's recruiter if unsure
Accept A today, since it pays £38,000 against about £11,538
options.why: You decided on pay alone, before checking a condition that could void the offer.

options.text: Accept B today, since London needs no work permission
options.why: You chose by the easy condition. A suits a trading career better if its condition can be met, so check it first.

options.text: Accept both, and decide in the summer
options.why: You held two acceptances. Accepting is a promise, and one of them would be broken.

feedback.correct: Check the open condition first, then weigh the return rate and the work.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the fact that could make an offer fall away.

explain.text: A conditional offer falls away if its condition fails, so the open one is checked first. A pays $3{,}800 \times 10 = 38{,}000$ pounds and B about $60{,}000 \times \tfrac{10}{52} \approx 11{,}538$, but the return rate and the work matter more here. Decide inside the 14 days, and withdraw from the rest once you accept.

items.title: Defending a number
items.prose: Your CV says: "Backtested a pairs trade on 8 years of daily prices; out-of-sample net Sharpe 0.6 after a 5 bp cost." The interviewer asks: "How did you choose the pairs?"
items.question: Which answer defends the line best?

options.text: "I picked the pairs on the first 4 years and tested on the last 4. The 0.6 comes from the last 4."
"I kept the 10 pairs that did best over all 8 years."
options.why: You chose the pairs on the data you tested on. Then 0.6 is not out of sample, and the next question finds it.

options.text: "I tried about 50 pairs, and the best one gave 0.6."
options.why: You reported the best of many tries. The best of 50 looks good even when nothing works.

options.text: "Pairs selection is standard; any sensible choice works."
options.why: You dodged the method. The interviewer asked how, so say what you did and on which data.

feedback.correct: Chosen on one period, tested on another: the 0.6 is out of sample.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the answer that keeps the test data out of the choice.

explain.text: Choosing pairs on one period and testing on another keeps the 0.6 out of sample. Choosing on all 8 years, or keeping the best of 50, puts the answer into the test. Prepare one sentence like this for every number on the CV.

items.title: A week of decisions
items.prose: Ana, an invented candidate, logs one busy week of her cycle. Scroll the table to the end.

rows: Sat a trading firm's real test link to see the format, planning to prepare afterwards
Sent a rolling-review application the day her CV was ready, though it closes in January
Listed six programming languages, four from one tutorial each, to pass keyword screens
Got an offer with a 14-day deadline and told her preferred firm the next morning
Skipped a hedge fund's research role, because a market maker sharing its name rejected her
Opened her "why us" draft with the firm's pay being the best
After a final-round rejection, sent one thankful line asking for one area to work on

items.question: Select all that apply: which entries are mistakes?

options.text: Monday: the real test link, to see the format
Monday: applying the day the CV was ready
options.why: That was right. Under rolling review the closing date is the last day, not the target.

options.text: Tuesday: six languages for the keyword screens
Wednesday: telling the preferred firm the next morning
options.why: That was right. Telling the other firm at once gives it the most time to speed up.

options.text: Thursday: skipping the hedge fund's role
Friday: opening "why us" with the pay
Friday: one short feedback request
options.why: That was right. One thankful line with one question is the request most likely to be answered.

feedback.correct: Four mistakes: the real link, the padded languages, the shared name and the pay.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each entry against what it costs: an attempt, trust, or a whole application.

explain.text: The real link is the attempt, and padded languages fail the first question in them. A shared name is not a shared firm, and pay is never the reason to give. The other three entries are the moves the course teaches.

items.title: A plan to July
items.prompt:
Amira, an invented candidate, is in the second year of a four-year MMath, graduating in 2029. She aims at trading and can work only in the UK. Today is 2 November 2026. These invented programmes are open.

| Programme | Who and where | Closes |
|---|---|---|
| P1, insight week | First-years; London | 8 Nov 2026 |
| P2, spring week | Class of 2029; London; rolling review | 6 Dec 2026 |
| P3, insight programme | Class of 2029; London | 3 Jan 2027 |
| P4, summer 2027 trader internship | Penultimate year; Amsterdam | Rolling |

Write her plan up to July 2027.

(a) Which programmes should she apply to, in what order? Why not the others?

(b) When does her main internship cycle open? How many full weeks does she have from today?

(c) A trading firm's reported process: 80 arithmetic items in 8 minutes, +1 and −1, no skipping. Then a recruiter call, then a market-making game and probability rounds. List what she prepares, with the app course that trains each.

(d) Give her two rules for the first real test link.
items.model:
**(a)** She is class of 2029 and two years from graduation, so P2 and P3 fit. P2 goes first: it closes sooner and reviews on a rolling basis, so she sends it this week. P3 follows well before 3 January. P1 is for first-years, and she is a second-year. P4 is for the penultimate year, her third, and it is in Amsterdam, where she cannot work.

**(b)** Her penultimate year is 2027 to 2028, so her main internship is summer 2028. Its postings open about 1 July 2027, with rolling review. From 2 November 2026 that is $28 + 31 + 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 1 = 241$ days. $241 = 7 \times 34 + 3$, so she has 34 full weeks.

**(c)**

| Stage | What she prepares | App course |
|---|---|---|
| Arithmetic test | Speed and accuracy, 6 seconds an item | Mental Maths Under Pressure |
| Recruiter call | A 45-second "why trading", and her six stories | Getting the Internship, levels 2 and 3 |
| Market-making game | Quoting a bid and an offer, and moving them | Market-Making Games |
| Probability rounds | Probability and expected value, reasoned aloud | Probability Puzzles |

Speed matters because a blind guess is worth $\tfrac14 - \tfrac34 = -0.5$, and with no skipping every item gets an answer. The faster she is, the fewer forced guesses she makes.

**(d)** First, the real link is never practice. She practises on mocks and any practice test first, because the first sitting counts. A retake may be months away. Second, she checks the set-up before the clock starts: the rules, the system check, a quiet room, the phone away, a charged laptop. If the connection drops, she screenshots the screen with the time and emails the recruiter at once.

rubric.text: Applies to P2 and P3, P2 first because it closes sooner under rolling review, with eligibility as the reason.
Rules out P1 (first-years only) and P4 (penultimate year, and no right to work there).
Places her main cycle at summer 2028, opening about 1 July 2027, and counts 34 full weeks (241 days).
Lists arithmetic under negative marking, a "why trading" answer, a market-making game and probability, each with its course.
Explains why speed matters: a blind guess is worth −0.5, and with no skipping every item is answered.
Gives two rules: the real link is never practice; check the set-up first, and screenshot and email if it breaks.

explain.text: Eligibility comes first, then dates, then a list of what each stage tests. The main cycle is a year ahead of the internship. The first real link is an attempt, never practice.

items.title: A disagreement in STAR form
items.prompt:
Notes on Chris, an invented candidate.

- Second-year group project, four students, forecasting daily electricity demand, two weeks before the deadline.
- His job was the validation.
- He found the model was tested on days it had been trained on. The forecast looked within 5% on 91% of days.
- He rebuilt the test on the last 3 months only, held out from training. The figure fell to 74%.
- The team wanted to report 91%. He showed both numbers at a meeting and proposed reporting 74%.
- The team agreed. The project scored 72%, and the marker praised the validation.

The question is "Tell me about a time you disagreed with your team."

(a) Write Chris's answer in STAR form, with one line of reflection. Keep it within two minutes aloud: at 130 words a minute, at most 260 words.

(b) Name the follow-up question you expect, and answer it in two sentences.
items.model:
**(a)** *Situation.* Last year I was in a four-person project forecasting daily electricity demand, two weeks before the deadline. *Task.* My job was the validation. *Action.* I found our model was being tested on days it had been trained on. On that test the forecast was within 5% on 91% of days. I rebuilt the test on the last three months only, held out from training. On those months the figure fell to 74%. The team wanted to keep the 91%, because it looked better. At our next meeting I showed both numbers side by side. I explained that only the held-out figure says how the model does on new days. I proposed we report 74% and say why. *Result.* The team agreed, and we submitted on time. The project scored 72%, and the marker praised the validation. *Reflection.* I now check how a test set was built before I trust any score.

That is about 150 words, a little over a minute aloud.

**(b)** Expected follow-up: "What would you do differently?" I would agree the test split on day one, before anyone had seen a score. The argument cost us a meeting we could have spent improving the model.

rubric.text: Opens with a real time: when, where and who, in the first sentence.
States his task: the validation was his job.
Gives his actions with "I": found the leak, rebuilt the test, showed both numbers, proposed the 74%.
Gives the result with numbers: 91% against 74%, the 72% mark and the marker's comment.
Reflects with a real habit, not a disguised strength or blame on the team.
Stays within 260 words, two minutes aloud.
Names a likely follow-up and answers it with one change or one fact.

explain.text: Half of a STAR answer goes on the actions, said with "I". The result carries numbers, and the reflection names a habit. Every story invites a follow-up, so know one fact beyond what you said.
